subject: system-design
question: Why is reading from memory generally faster than reading from disk?
options: Memory stores less data per byte
Disks can only be read by one process
Memory is always located on another machine
RAM access takes nanoseconds, while disk access takes microseconds to milliseconds
explanation: This large gap is why caches keep hot data in memory.

subject: system-design
question: What is latency?
options: The time taken to complete a single request
The number of requests processed per second
The percentage of requests that succeed
The number of concurrent connections open
explanation: Latency measures how long one operation takes, usually in milliseconds.

subject: system-design
question: What is throughput?
options: The time taken by one request from start to finish
The delay between a DNS lookup and a TCP connect
The largest message size a server accepts
The amount of work completed per unit of time
explanation: Throughput is a rate, such as requests or megabytes processed per second.

subject: system-design
question: What does a p99 latency of 200 ms mean?
options: The server handles 200 requests per second
The average request takes 99 ms
99% of requests complete within 200 ms
1% of requests failed with a timeout
explanation: Percentile latency describes the tail of the distribution, which often matters more than the average.

subject: system-design
question: What is bandwidth?
options: The maximum amount of data that can be transferred per unit of time
The number of servers in a data center
The time a single packet takes to reach its destination
The percentage of requests that fail
explanation: Bandwidth is capacity, such as megabits per second, while latency is delay.

subject: system-design
question: What is the typical effect of batching many requests together?
options: Lower latency and lower throughput at the same time
Lower latency, but throughput drops to zero
Higher throughput, but each individual request may wait longer
No effect on either latency or throughput
explanation: Batching amortizes per-request overhead, but each request may wait for the batch to fill.

subject: system-design
question: Why does physical distance between a user and a data center affect latency?
options: Longer distances cause packets to be compressed
Signals take time to travel the distance, adding round-trip delay
Distant servers always have slower CPUs
Physical distance changes the database schema
explanation: Propagation delay is bounded by the speed of light in fiber, so distance sets a floor on round-trip time.

subject: system-design
question: Which change most directly reduces latency for users far from the origin server?
options: Adding more log lines to every request
Serving content from a location closer to those users
Increasing the number of automatic retries
Removing all caching from the request path
explanation: Moving data closer to users cuts propagation distance, which dominates for distant clients.
